newsitem.title: KENYA: Africans want higher coffee prices to help growth.
newsitem.headline: Africans want higher coffee prices to help growth.

text.p: Declining global coffee prices are damaging Africa at a time when industry reforms of the last several years are starting to bear fruit, an executive at the Inter-Africa Coffee Organisation (IACO) said on Wednesday.

Donald Kaberuka told Reuters in an interview in Nairobi that African producers wanted an emergency gathering of the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) to agree tangible solutions to stem the decline.
"The declining prices have come at a wrong time for Africa. It is a time reforms and adjustments were just beginning to bear fruit," said Kaberuka, economist at the Abidjan-based IACO.

"It is damaging to African economies. Over the last two years, African countries have been getting an average of $2.8 billion from (coffee) exports. This year, and with current price trends, that figure could drop to $1.5 billion," he added.
Coffee is a major foreign exchange earner for several countries in east, central and western Africa.
Kaberuka named Uganda as one of the countries in which reforms had led to massive gains. Authorities there said procurement rose to a record 4.2 million bags in 1995/96.
Ethiopia and Kenya have also reported recent improvements.
Kaberuka said Africa had put forward proposals on how to reverse the decline, to be discussed at an emergency session of the ACPC in Brazil on January 23. He gave no further details.

But Ugandan coffee sources said they sought an additional cut of 2.5 million bags in the first six months of 1997 on total exports of 53.5 million bags agreed by ACPC in May. They said that Colombia had put forward a figure of around 2.6 million.

Other African proposals included applying "diplomatic and political pressure" on big Asian and Pacific producers -- such as Vietnam and Guatemala -- to join the pact in order to make its results more effective, according to a Tanzanian official.
European brokers have said Vietnam's joining was unlikely.
Senior Ugandan industry officials said African presence at an Asian International Coffee conference would have as its main focus putting significant pressure on Vietnam to join.

Kaberuka said the current limitations plan had had very limited success in the 1996/97 period. It had brought down investories held by consumers substantially but had failed to maintain market prices at renumerative levels for producers.

He said there was no big coffee surplus on the coffee market for this year. But he added that as a result of seasonal factors, an excess of surplus was expected in the January-June period in 1997. The excess levels were still to be determined.
"We have reached the conclusion that we need a revision or adjustment of the current plan for the remainder of the period. Exact methods are to be discussed," Kaberuka said.
Kaberuka said current trends would put a lot of pressure on coffee, especially robustas, but would not give specific details on account of jeopardising Africa's bargaining position.
